Support for Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, and local models.

2. Ask Opus 5.5 to explain every agent in plain English so you understand how decisions are made.

3. Choose your models and configure your API keys. Use stronger models for critical decisions and cheaper ones for less demanding tasks.

4. Start with one ticker you understand. Read the full bull-versus-bear debate before trusting any output.

5. Run the built-in backtest over the last 3 years, including realistic fees and slippage. If it can't outperform buy-and-hold after costs, investigate before going further.

6. Explore broker integration, such as Alpaca for stocks or Binance for crypto.

7. Add strict safeguards: fixed position sizing, stop-loss rules, daily loss limits, and an emergency kill switch.

8. Run it in paper-trading mode for at least two weeks. Compare its performance with the backtest.

9. Connect Telegram for decision alerts. Only consider live trading after thorough testing, starting with an amount you can afford to lose.

items.title: Agentic AI Raises New Questions for Financial Institutions
items.summary:
DownloadDownload

Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved beyond answering questions and generating content. Increasingly, AI systems are being designed to act. Agentic AI can pursue objectives, make decisions and take actions on a user’s behalf, potentially with limited human involvement in individual decisions. [...] Consider a customer who gives an AI agent access to a bank account with an instruction to manage the customer’s cash efficiently. The agent decides to transfer funds, convert currencies or purchase an investment.

At first sight, these may appear to be ordinary customer transactions. Agentic AI, however, exposes important distinctions between identity, authentication, authority and attribution. [...] As agentic AI becomes more capable, firms may increasingly encounter interactions in which an AI agent collects information, compares products and initiates transactions for a customer. That creates a new layer between the institution and the person or entity with whom it has established a customer relationship.

items.title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips | TechCrunch
items.summary:
The chip launch comes as hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, and even AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own lines of AI-specific semiconductors and accompanying software in order to reduce their reliance on the dominance of Nvidia.

The news also comes at a particularly vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend admitted to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy. [...] Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries. [...] TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post. The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote.

Để giải bài toán tích phân này, chúng ta cần tìm nguyên hàm của hàm số \( f(x) = x^2 \). Nguyên hàm của \( x^2 \) là một hàm số \( F(x) \) sao cho \( F'(x) = x^2 \).

Nguyên hàm của \( x^2 \) là:
\[ \int x^2 \, dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + C \]
trong đó \( C \) là hằng số tích phân.

items.title: A school hired a photographer to take pictures of its students. Police say he used those pictures to make AI-generated c
items.summary:
A school hired a photographer to take pictures of its students. Police say he used those pictures to make AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Two days after a tip came in, they arrested him.

How did police find out what was happening to those photos in the first place?

The photographer was Russell Bloodworth. According to one family’s lawsuit, he photographed their daughter at school four times. She was under five.

On June 8, police in Bentonville, Arkansas, got a tip about a Grok account. Two days later, they searched Bloodworth’s home. On his phone, they found a hidden folder with around 1,700 photos and videos.

While reviewing the material, a detective found a photo from a professional shoot. He later identified the girl in it as someone who’d attended one of Bloodworth’s summer photography classes.

The detective could spot a few AI images by eye. Most looked real enough that he said he needed forensic software to tell how they’d been made. Police seized more than 60 devices. Bloodworth pleaded not guilty.

The original report came from xAI, the company that built Grok. xAI says it reported the activity on April 23 to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children. More than six weeks passed between that report and the tip reaching Bentonville police.

Then xAI sued Bloodworth. It asked a judge to make him pay for its defense in lawsuits tied to his alleged conduct.

In October, the girl and her mom sued both of them. According to their lawsuit, the mom learned what had happened to her daughter’s school photos when Homeland Security contacted her.

If someone uploaded your kid’s school portrait to an AI, how the f#ck would you ever find out?

items.summary: Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. [...] Using our embodied reasoning model (Gemini Robotics ER) to keep track of the workflow, and the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model to control its hands and arms, the robot reaches into supply bins, picks up metal automotive brackets, and places them into sequencing containers, all while correcting for any gaps. Achieving a 96% success rate, this pilot shows promising progress toward widespread real-world industrial applications. Path Robotics, an Ohio startup that builds AI to let robots weld, has raised $300m in a Series E round at a $2.45bn valuation. Georgian, an AI-focused growth equity firm, led the round, the company said. The deal nearly quadruples Path’s valuation, Bloomberg reported. [...] Path’s AI model, Obsidian, lets robots find weld joints, plan the welds and adjust as conditions change, instead of following fixed programs. The company says its annual recurring revenue grew 17-fold in the past 18 months. Customers include shipbuilder HII, Lockheed Martin and Saronic, which makes autonomous vessels for the military.

> “Our goal isn’t to automate one step, but to automate the entire factory,” said Andy Lonsberry, co-founder and chief executive of Path Robotics. [...] One new form is Rove, which puts Obsidian on a Boston Dynamics quadruped so it can weld parts where they stand. Path is working to fill 50 preorders for Rove, Lonsberry told Bloomberg. items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.
